slides.0.title: Styles, classification and labels
slides.0.subtitle: Qualitätswein, Prädikat, DAC and reading a label
slides.1.title: The quality ladder and KMW
slides.1.highlights.0.title: What KMW is
slides.1.highlights.0.content: KMW (Klosterneuburger Mostwaage) is Austria's must-weight scale; it differs from Germany's Oechsle and values cannot be swapped directly
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Wein and Landwein
slides.1.highlights.1.content: "Wein" replaced Tafelwein in 2009; Landwein needs at least 14 °KMW
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Qualitätswein
slides.1.highlights.2.content: At least 15 °KMW; from a single specified region and officially tested
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Kabinett is not a Prädikat
slides.1.highlights.3.content: In Austria Kabinett is a subcategory of Qualitätswein (at least 17 °KMW, dry, no chaptalisation), not a Prädikatswein
slides.1.content: This is one of the biggest differences from Germany, where Kabinett is a Prädikat.
slides.2.title: The Prädikatswein levels
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Spätlese and Auslese
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Spätlese needs at least 19 °KMW; Auslese at least 21 °KMW
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Strohwein
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Strohwein/Schilfwein need at least 25 °KMW
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Trockenbeerenauslese
slides.2.highlights.2.content: At least 30 °KMW; sources differ on the minimum for Ausbruch, which Level 2 handles from the regulation itself
slides.2.highlights.3.title: No chaptalisation
slides.2.content: KMW thresholds: Kabinett 17, Spätlese 19, Auslese 21, BA 25, TBA 30. Figures are compiled from Wikipedia; the official wine law prevails.
slides.3.title: Sweetness and label basics
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Sweetness terms
slides.3.highlights.0.content: trocken (dry), halbtrocken (medium dry), lieblich (medium sweet) and süß (sweet), following the EU sweetness categories
slides.3.highlights.1.title: What a label usually shows
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Producer, vintage, variety, region or DAC, quality level (e.g. Qualitätswein, Spätlese), alcohol and the Ried name for a single vineyard
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Official testing and the seal
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Qualitätswein must be tested and carries a state test number; a red-white-red strip is commonly seen on the closure
slides.3.content: Level 2 covers DAC labelling (Klassik/Reserve) and Ried in detail.
slides.4.title: A first look at DAC and Sekt Austria
slides.4.highlights.0.title: DAC: defined by regional style
slides.4.highlights.0.content: A DAC wine must meet the region's variety, style and quality rules; the label may simply carry the region name
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Sekt Austria
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Austria's sparkling quality pyramid with three tiers — Klassik, Reserve and Große Reserve (since 2015); details in Level 3
slides.4.content: For Level 1 you only need: DAC = regional style; Sekt Austria = three sparkling tiers.
In Austria, which category does Kabinett belong to?
In Austria the Prädikat levels start at Spätlese; Kabinett sits within Qualitätswein.
A. A unit of alcohol strength
B. A unit of grape-must sugar (must weight)
C. A unit of residual sugar
KMW is Austria's must-weight scale, different from Germany's Oechsle.
Which of these may not be chaptalised?
Prädikatswein may not be chaptalised, and neither may Kabinett.
